newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA AIMS TO PRIVATISE SUNAIR BY EARLY 1997.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA AIMS TO PRIVATISE SUNAIR BY EARLY 1997.

text.p: The South African government hopes to complete the privatisation of former homeland airline Sunair by early next year, Public Enterprises Minister Stella Sigcau said on Monday. "I am positive that...in the new year we will see actual implementation (of the sale of Sunair)," she told a media briefing.
Part of the proceeds of the sale would be used to retire state debt with the rest used for development programmes, such as pilot training.
She gave no details on the likely buyer for Sunair but said negotiations between unions and management were proceeding well regarding the airline's structure.

In September Virgin Atlantic Airways announced a new code sharing pact with Sunair, and Virgin owner Richard Branson said he was interested in buying the state-owned carrier to develop it into a "pan-African" low-cost regional carrier.
Sigcau said that since the release of the government's macro-economic strategy and a transport "white paper" it was now possible to speed up the restructuring of state assets.
"We were operating in a vacuum before," she said.
South African Airways was being urged to "move forward as quickly as possible" with the aim of finding a strategic equity partner, she added.
But before that SAA had to be repositioned and made either a subsidiary of state transport group Transnet or a stand-alone company.

Elsewhere, Sigau said telecommunications utility Telkom was fairly advanced in identifying a strategic equity partner. The company last month issued a shortlist of seven companies interested in taking a 30 percent stake in the concern.
Government sources said due diligence investigations into Telkom by these parties was now nearing completion and a further shorter shortlist could be issued in the next week or so.

Among other state concerns Sigcau said port operator Portnet had to improve its ability to handle increased trade flows and a key question was to decide whether its infrastructure and operational divisions should be separate entities.
Railways company Spoornet had to reposition itself over the next three years as a a market-driven freight carrier as a opposed to a low cost transport provider, she added.
Progress on South African privatisation is seen as a litmus test of the government's commitment to economic reform.
